title: Shopify Theme Architecture — Directory Structure & Hierarchy
content: Official Shopify theme architecture (from shopify.dev). A theme controls an online store's organisation, features, and style through a standard directory structure. DIRECTORY STRUCTURE: assets/ (images, CSS, JavaScript — supports .liquid extension), blocks/ (theme blocks — standalone Liquid files for reusable modules), config/ (settings files for theme editor), layout/ (base templates — theme.liquid is mandatory), locales/ (translation files), sections/ (reusable content modules and section groups), snippets/ (reusable Liquid code), templates/ (page-specific templates — JSON or Liquid). Only layout/theme.liquid is mandatory for upload. COMPONENT HIERARCHY (top to bottom): Layout → Template → Section Group → Section → Block → Snippet. FILE CATEGORIES: (1) Markup/features — Liquid-based layout and functionality files. (2) Supporting assets — images, CSS, JavaScript, locale files. (3) Config files — JSON configuration data for theme editor customisation. TEMPLATE-SPECIFIC CSS: Output the template object in the body class (<body class='template-{{ template.name }}'>) then target in CSS (.template-product { ... }). FIGMA IMPLICATION: When designing Shopify storefronts in Figma, mirror this hierarchy in your layer structure. Each page design should be a Layout frame containing a Template frame, which contains Section frames, which contain Block frames. This 1:1 mapping between Figma layers and Shopify architecture makes developer handoff precise and reduces implementation ambiguity.

title: Shopify Theme Layouts — Base Templates & Required Objects
content: Official Shopify layout documentation (from shopify.dev). Layouts are the base of the theme through which all templates render. They are Liquid files enabling content reuse across multiple page types — typically including <head> elements, headers, and footers. FILE LOCATION: layout/ directory. Default file is theme.liquid (mandatory). LAYOUT TYPES: General (applies to all non-checkout pages) and Checkout (Shopify Plus only — checkout.liquid is deprecated for Thank You and Order Status pages, sunset August 28, 2025). REQUIRED LIQUID OBJECTS: (1) content_for_header — must be placed inside HTML <head> tag. Dynamically loads all scripts required by Shopify (hCaptcha, apps, etc.). Should not be modified or parsed. (2) content_for_layout — dynamically outputs content for each template. Must be placed between <body> tags. Both objects are required — omitting either prevents file saving via code editor or CLI. SPECIFYING LAYOUTS: JSON templates use the 'layout' attribute in schema. Liquid templates use the 'layout' Liquid tag. FIGMA IMPLICATION: In Figma, the layout maps to your persistent page elements — header, footer, announcement bar. Design these as shared components that appear on every page frame. The 'content_for_layout' area is the variable zone between header and footer where template-specific content goes. Always design header and footer as separate component instances, not drawn into each page.

title: Shopify Theme Templates — Types, JSON vs Liquid & Naming
content: Official Shopify template documentation (from shopify.dev). Templates control what renders on each page type. TEMPLATE FILE TYPES: (1) JSON templates (.json) — data files that allow merchants to add, remove, and rearrange sections through theme editor. HTML and Liquid code must be in referenced sections. Preferred for merchant flexibility and editor performance. (2) Liquid templates (.liquid) — Liquid markup files where you add code directly without section requirements. JSON templates are preferred when using sections. TEMPLATE TYPES: 404 (error page), article (blog post), blog (blog listing), cart (shopping cart), collection (product listing), gift_card.liquid (Liquid-only), index (homepage), list-collections (all collections), page (shop pages — About, Contact), password (password protection), product (product detail), search (search results), metaobject (custom content types). Five types require Liquid format exclusively: gift_card, robots.txt, agents.md, llms.txt, llms-full.txt. Maximum 1000 JSON templates per theme across all types. CONTENT REQUIREMENT: Each template must include objects matching its purpose — a product template must always include the product object and product form tag. FIGMA IMPLICATION: Design a Figma frame for each template type your store needs. At minimum: index (homepage), product, collection, cart, page, 404, search. Name your Figma frames to match template names (e.g. 'template-product', 'template-collection') for clear developer handoff. Each frame represents the content_for_layout zone — header and footer come from the layout component.

title: Shopify Sections — Reusable Content Modules, Schema & Rendering
content: Official Shopify sections documentation (from shopify.dev). Sections are Liquid files enabling merchants to create reusable modules of content that can be customised. Each section accommodates up to 50 blocks. FILE LOCATION: sections/ directory. CORE COMPONENTS: (1) Main content — HTML and Liquid accessing global objects, tags, filters, plus section-specific objects (section object for properties/settings, block object for block properties/settings). Variables are scoped within their section. (2) Assets — custom JavaScript and stylesheets via {% javascript %} and {% stylesheet %} tags. (3) Schema — {% schema %} tag defines: name, tag, class, limit, settings, blocks, max_blocks, presets, defaults, locales, enabled_on, disabled_on. RENDERING METHODS: (1) Dynamic — reference in JSON templates or section groups (preferred). (2) Static — use Liquid section tag (discouraged). (3) Section Rendering API — AJAX-based rendering. PRESETS: Section and block files must define presets in their schema to support being added to JSON templates. APP BLOCKS: Sections can accommodate app blocks — include { 'type': '@app' } in schema. THEME EDITOR: Editor dynamically modifies DOM without full page reloads. FIGMA IMPLICATION: Each section in your Figma design should be a distinct frame with clear boundaries — full-width background with content constrained to the container width. Name section frames descriptively (e.g. 'section-hero', 'section-featured-collection', 'section-newsletter'). Design sections to be self-contained and independently reorderable — no section should depend on the one above or below it for visual coherence.

title: Shopify Blocks — Theme Blocks, Section Blocks, App Blocks & Nesting
content: Official Shopify blocks documentation (from shopify.dev). Blocks are reusable modules within sections. Each block maintains individual settings and can be added, removed, and reordered. THREE BLOCK TYPES: (1) Theme blocks — standalone Liquid files in /blocks folder. Maximum flexibility: can restrict sections to specific block types, permit nesting, and create static blocks (fixed position, can be hidden but not deleted). (2) Section blocks — defined within a section's {% schema %} tag. Cannot be nested. Work exclusively within parent section. Cannot coexist with theme blocks in the same section. (3) App blocks — provided by installed Shopify apps (reviews, custom forms, etc.). Require explicit schema support ({ 'type': '@app' }). BLOCKS VS SNIPPETS: Theme blocks display settings in theme editor and allow merchant customisation. Snippets handle repeatable markup without merchant customisation. Blocks cannot receive variables from parent code; snippets can. Use blocks for structure and settings, snippets for reusable markup. BEST PRACTICES (from sections-blocks best practices): Use blocks for granular customisation within sections when it enhances usability. BLOCK LAYOUTS: Vertical stacking for text-based content requiring hierarchy. Horizontal stacking when hierarchy is not necessary — stack horizontally or create adaptive grids. Responsive: allow blocks to wrap across multiple lines or offer sliding controls for narrow viewports. Do not squeeze blocks into constrained spaces. Do not rely on a specific block type or sequence to design a layout. FLEXIBILITY: Group related settings into blocks to reduce complexity rather than creating separate blocks for each attribute. Nest theme settings within blocks. Group elements following specific hierarchies together. FIGMA IMPLICATION: Design blocks as small, self-contained Figma components that can be nested inside section components. Each block variant should work independently of surrounding blocks. Test block reordering in your Figma prototype to verify layouts hold up regardless of block sequence.
